headline: Strong opportunity in Australian private credit: seeing deals banks would have done in a heartbeat, not seen in nine years, with margins set to increase as credit crunch deepens
reasoning: Paul Miron argues that private credit in Australia is presenting exceptional opportunities not seen in the past nine years. He notes that the quality of deals now available — conservative, low-risk transactions that banks would historically have taken — is what excites him most, not just the return. He expects a credit crunch in the sector to increase over time, which will push margins higher, rewarding those already positioned in the market. He emphasises that private credit is fundamentally about capital preservation, not return maximisation, and that investors need to reassess their risk frameworks accordingly.
quote: I am seeing opportunities in debt that I have not seen last nine years. Yeah, right. And it's not. The return that I'm really excited about is the type of deals the banks would have done in a heartbeat. And we're seeing those opportunities on the desk right now. That is what makes me quite excited. And what will happen is those really low conservative type deals are available. But then over time, as the credit crunch, I believe in the sector will increase, the margins start increasing. So being in the market, understanding it is where the opportunity is.
episode_title: When the credit crunch meets the housing crunch

headline: Credit crunch developing specifically in property development lending; rationale to develop is the weakest in 30 years and commencements outlook is poor
reasoning: Miron distinguishes between the broader $3.6 trillion Australian lending market — where $200 billion of private credit is a small share — and the specific slice funding property development, where a credit crunch is actively forming. Capital allocated to property development will become far harder to access, which will exacerbate supply shortages. The macro rationale to develop hasn't been this weak in 30 years, with builders and developers failing in increasing numbers. He says investors with too much exposure to this sector face materially elevated risk, though the situation is not permanent.
quote: private credit, in the big scheme of lending, it's $200 billion across $3.6 trillion worth of lending in Australia. So it's a very small proportion where you'll have a credit crunch is the type of lending or liquidity of capital. So the amount of capital that will be allocated in the economy for property development is going to get a lot harder. So there will be a probably credit crunch in that area, which is going to exacerbate the supply. So the next thing you're going to see is how many properties are commencing. I think that is not not looking very good. Just the macroeconomic, the rationale to actually develop as a property developer at the moment probably hasn't been weaker than in the last 30 years.

headline: Now is the opportunity in private credit — bad loans were written last year, not now; but capital preservation must be the priority, not return maximisation
reasoning: Miron invokes Howard Marks' principle that bad loans in a cycle are written during the boom, not after the correction, to argue that the entry point for private credit is now attractive. He cautions that investors need to be far more educated about what they are investing in, with risk-reward and capital preservation as the primary lens rather than yield maximisation. He draws a parallel with global bond markets repricing risk as the world economy shows fragility, noting investors are demanding higher returns across the board. The opportunity exists but requires selectivity and due diligence on the borrower.
quote: I think one better is Howard Marx. In private credit. The bad loans were written last year. Not not now. So I think now is the opportunity is just talking to the right people. But investors need to investors need to be a lot more educated in relation to what they're investing in. The risk the risk reward has to be the front line. The private credit is all about preservation of capital. It's not about maximizing your return. So I think that is a really important point in relation to investors to really take, take a deep breath and actually reassess it.

Government spending also needs to come under control as a longer-term consideration.

In his view, what actually saves us from what saves us at the moment is that unemployment is very sticky. So it's not it's not really going to go up too high. headline: Paul Miron warns private credit investors against construction and development lending as rising costs and falling end-markets make capital loss risks too high relative to extra return
reasoning: Miron has been telling clients for nearly a decade that construction lending carries risks that may not be worth the additional rate premium. He says the last four years have seen construction economics become harder than ever, with costs rising, land prices inelastic and end-market values falling around 10%, making it very difficult for developers to profit. For private credit lenders exposed to this segment, the possibility of losing capital is significantly higher, and investors need to assess whether extra yield justifies that risk. He distinguishes this from short-term income-focused lending which is more dynamic and less exposed to the underlying asset's value.
quote: Right now, in the last four years, it's been harder than it's ever been before. The economics of building or developing has never been harder. Construction costs are going high. Land is inelastic, doesn't really fall. Um, and the end market has fallen by 10% at the moment. So it's very difficult for a property developer to actually make profit on a, on a transaction. And so if you're a private credit lender and lending money to that transaction, your your possibility of a losing your capital is significantly higher. and you really need to ask yourself, is it worth the extra risk to get that extra little bit of return?
episode_title: Property downturn reveals private credit cracks
